harmonics.aim: How can a few angular field patterns combine to produce directional radiation?
harmonics.read: Each point in the diagram stands for a direction of observation. In Radiation pattern the distance from the origin represents intensity; the surface is therefore a graph, rather than a material body. On the unit sphere removes that change in radius. Its colours show intensity and its arrows show the electric field at the selected phase. Compare the same direction in both views before interpreting a lobe or a dark region.
harmonics.engineering: Consider two modes that give equal electric-field amplitudes at the backward detector. If their phases differ by 180°, their fields cancel there. The same modes can reinforce at another angle. It would be incorrect to add the two intensity diagrams: that would lose precisely the interference that produces the directional effect. Changing the common phase rotates all instantaneous arrows through the oscillation without changing the intensity pattern. The relative phase of the modes can change the pattern.

plane.aim: Why does a plane wave need more spherical-wave terms as the region of interest grows?
plane.read: The intended incident wave is the same in every calculation. What changes is the number of terms used to represent it. Inspect Along the beam axis together with Error vs distance: a nearly straight wavefront can conceal a small amplitude or phase error. The centre of the map usually converges before its outer boundary.
plane.engineering: Imagine using the expansion to illuminate a particle of radius a. It must be accurate over the whole particle, not just at the origin. Halving the wavelength doubles ka, so a truncation that was adequate before may now fail at the particle surface. Build up adds terms with the amplitudes required by the plane wave; it does not add extra light sources. Enough for view estimates a useful truncation for the displayed region. It is a numerical check, rather than a new law of wave propagation.

rayleigh.aim: When is an induced electric dipole enough to describe a particle, and what does that imply for a suspension?
rayleigh.read: The polar diagram separates the two electric-field components relative to the scattering plane. Forward scattering is at 0° and backward scattering at 180°. A missing component at 90° is a polarization effect; it is not necessarily a dark direction for unpolarized illumination. Zoom changes the drawing scale. Use cross sections when comparing the scattered powers of different particles.
rayleigh.engineering: For a small sphere of fixed optical contrast, scattering grows as a⁶, whereas its material volume grows as a³. If all radii are doubled at the same particle volume fraction, the number concentration falls by eight but the scattering cross section of each particle rises by 64. The suspension therefore scatters eight times more strongly per unit path length. Absorption has a different size dependence. This is why two dispersions with the same mass concentration can have very different turbidity. Close to a metal resonance, check the exact Mie result as well: neither optical contrast nor the validity of the dipole approximation can be inferred from diameter alone.

mie.aim: Which features require more than an electric dipole?
mie.read: Follow one change in particle size while keeping the refractive indices fixed. The angular distribution, integrated cross sections and multipole contributions are different ways of examining the same solution. A peak in an efficiency curve need not correspond to the brightest feature at every observation angle.
mie.engineering: An efficiency of four means that the removed power equals the incident irradiance multiplied by four times the geometrical area. It does not mean that four photons are removed for every incident photon. The field is disturbed outside the geometrical outline, and extinction includes interference between the incident wave and the forward-scattered field. As the sphere grows, the phase varies across it and higher multipoles become important. Inspecting their separate contributions can explain a new resonance; the total field must still be formed with their correct relative phases.

large.aim: How do the familiar ideas of reflection, refraction and diffraction emerge from the wave solution?
large.read: At large size parameter the forward lobe can be much brighter than the rest of the pattern. Compare the complete angular graph with a magnified region before deciding that a weak feature is absent. The 60 dB and 80 dB display ranges make weaker intensities visible; they do not add scattering power.
large.engineering: A water drop can be much larger than the wavelength and still show interference fringes. Geometrical rays locate features such as the primary rainbow, while the wave solution describes their finite width and surrounding oscillations. Use the water-drop setup near 142°, focus the detector direction and then increase the far-field magnification. The displayed colours encode intensity at one wavelength. A photograph of a white-light rainbow would require a spectral calculation and a colour transformation. Very narrow features also require enough angular samples; magnifying an under-resolved mesh cannot recover them.

real.aim: How do measured material properties turn a scattering calculation into a prediction for a colloid?
real.read: The wavelength axis is a vacuum wavelength. The material and surrounding medium together determine both the relative refractive index and the size parameter. For a coated particle, keep core diameter and shell thickness separate: the outer diameter is their sum with twice the shell thickness.
real.engineering: A small gold sphere removes green light mainly by absorption, so a dilute dispersion can look red in transmission while remaining visually clear. A larger sphere can scatter strongly enough to look quite different under front illumination. Increasing concentration changes the optical depth, not the isolated-particle cross section. Size spread averages cross sections over different particles and can broaden a spectrum. Size-dependent electron scattering changes the metal response itself. These are different effects: compare them separately before combining them or using either to explain an experimental linewidth.

design.aim: Which particle structures can produce a specified transmission colour, and how unique is the answer?
design.read: Choose the target first, then choose the candidate families. Every candidate is a particle geometry together with a concentration. Families compares the best result in each family; Colour map shows how a result changes within one family. The smallest colour difference is a statement about the chosen source, observer and measurement geometry.
design.engineering: Two different extinction spectra can give almost the same three colour coordinates under one light source. They may separate under another source or when scattering is collected differently. A small colour difference therefore does not identify a unique particle. Compare nearby designs, their concentration and the sensitivity to size spread before choosing a formulation. Select all and Deselect all refer to the candidate families, not to the samples already in the Lightbox. If electron scattering is enabled, the same correction is used throughout the search and retained when a candidate is sent to the Lightbox.

tmat.aim: What changes when the incident field at a particle includes light scattered by another particle?
tmat.read: Compare the interacting calculation with the independent-particle reference at the same geometry. The illuminating field at each sphere is found as part of the solution. A change in resonance or directionality should therefore be compared with the uncoupled reference, rather than with a single sphere placed somewhere else.
tmat.engineering: There are two meanings of multiple scattering in this app. For a small cluster, fields scattered between identified spheres retain their phases and can interfere. The T-matrix calculation follows these coherent interactions. In a macroscopic colloid, the Lightbox instead follows intensity transport through many randomly positioned particles. Adding the intensities of two isolated spheres cannot replace the cluster calculation, and treating an entire vial as one coherent cluster would also be inappropriate. Keeping these scales separate is essential when interpreting aggregation.

chain.aim: How do particle spacing, polarization and chain length alter the optical response?
chain.read: Start with a pair and specify the field direction relative to the line of centres. Gap means surface-to-surface gap; the centre spacing is one diameter plus that gap for equal spheres. Compare the response per sphere as chain length changes, so that simply adding more material is not confused with stronger coupling.
chain.engineering: A field along a chain drives a different charge arrangement from a field across it. Bringing the spheres together changes how the field from one sphere excites its neighbours, so the resonance can shift even though the individual particles are unchanged. A distribution of sphere sizes adds another source of broadening. Each sampled bead uses its own metal dimensions in the electron-scattering correction. The local optical model does not include electron tunnelling or charge transfer across a very small gap; a computed enhancement in that limit should not be interpreted as a measured prediction.

museum.aim: What must be specified before two scattering calculations, or a calculation and a measurement, can be compared?
museum.read: Read the axes and Paper settings before adjusting the overlay. Orientation and phase matter for field arrows; polarization and radial scale matter for angular diagrams. Spectra require a further distinction between cross section, decadic optical density and a normalized curve. A good registration of two drawings is not yet a test of their physics.
museum.engineering: The historical comparisons make some otherwise hidden assumptions visible. The B&H water examples change when their original optical constants are replaced by another compilation. Müller’s silver calculation retained only one electric multipole. Evanoff’s ordinate contains the decadic factor 1/ln(10). A fitted concentration can bring an experimental amplitude into agreement without validating its absolute value. Use the lesson link to vary a stated setting, and ask which independent observation would distinguish that explanation from the alternatives. A better modern fit does not, by itself, establish an error in an earlier author’s code.
